PSYC 559 Final Project: Predicting Daily Life Satisfaction on Gaming Days

Group 1

2026-11-26

How to run this file. This one file is the whole analysis. Knit it from start to finish; no other script has to be run first. It reads four files from the data/ folder next to it:

  • openesm_0075.rds, the Open Play daily diary from openESM. If it is missing, the download chunk downloads and saves it (this needs the internet).
  • survey_intake.csv.gz, the Open Play intake survey from the project’s repository (https://github.com/digital-wellbeing/open-play), which supplies the demographics.
  • game_classification.csv and game_classification_excluded.csv, the hand-reviewed lookup files that give each game title’s genre.

The file cleans the diary, builds the daily table, runs the clustering and the principal components, fits every supervised model on feature sets A and B, and saves the results to output/final_results.rds for the report. Fitting the models takes most of the knit time.

The test set stays locked until the final model is chosen. The chunks that touch the test set only run when run_test_set is TRUE. Keep it FALSE while reading the cross-validated comparison (Section 8), then set it to TRUE for one final knit.

run_test_set <- TRUE

Saved model fits. Each train() result is saved to output/model_fits/ as soon as it is fit. If the folder is missing, every model is fit from scratch. Later knits read the saved fit instead of refitting, so editing the text or the tables does not cost another long run: with the saved fits a knit takes a few minutes, and refitting every model took about 1.5 hours on a laptop with the folds in parallel. Set refit_models to TRUE (or delete the folder) whenever anything before Section 8 changes, and once more for the knit that is submitted (the handout: “knit clean before submitting”). The fits are exactly reproducible with the same package versions (Section 12), so that knit should give the same numbers.

refit_models <- FALSE
library(openesm)     # get_dataset() and cite()
library(dplyr)      # data manipulation and the pipe
library(tidyr)       # pivot_longer()
library(ggplot2)     # plots
library(naniar)      # vis_miss() and gg_miss_var()
library(rsample)     # group_initial_split()
library(recipes)     # imputation, dummy coding, and scaling inside the pipeline
library(cluster)     # silhouette()
library(caret)       # train(), groupKFold(), resamples(), varImp()
library(glmnet)      # elastic net
library(ranger)      # random forests
library(doParallel)  # fits the cross-validation folds in parallel

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Every file is read from data/ and written to output/, both in the folder
# that holds this Rmd. Knitting runs from that folder, and so does running
# chunks by hand after opening the .Rproj.
data_path <- function(file) file.path("data", file)
out_path  <- function(file) file.path("output", file)
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)

1. Research Questions

Supervised. Using same-day predictors and stable person characteristics from the intake survey, how well can we predict a player’s life satisfaction on a day they played video games? Life satisfaction is the daily item “I was satisfied with my life today,” rated on a 0 to 100 slider, so the target is continuous. The predictors are:

  • the six Basic Needs in Games (BANGS) items about the most recent session;
  • the type of game played and who the person played with that day;
  • sleep quality, the type of day, and the platform;
  • whether a stressful event occurred, which kinds, and how stressful the worst one was;
  • six daily basic-needs items (satisfaction and frustration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness);
  • demographics and life circumstances from the intake survey: age, gender, employment, education, relationship status, and caring for children.

Every daily predictor comes from the same day’s survey as the target, so the model describes what goes together on a day. It does not forecast. Affective valence (“How are you feeling right now?”) is not a predictor. It is answered in the same sitting and correlates highly with life satisfaction (Section 3).

The users are designers of digital well-being tools, such as a check-in at the end of a play session that flags players who may be having a bad day.

Unsupervised.

  • Dimensions of a day (PCA). We reduce the six daily basic-needs items. We expect two components, general satisfaction and general frustration, rather than one per need.
  • Types of play days (K-means). We cluster the play days on the six BANGS items, which describe the day’s most recent gaming session. The proposal expected days built around a “toxic competitive session,” a “low improvement session,” and a “satisfying solo session.”

The diary is the get_dataset("0075") output, downloaded once and saved to data/openesm_0075.rds.

The codebook

The codebook comes with the data, one row per variable. The item wording is in details and the response codes are in labels.

codebook <- open_play$metadata$features[[1]]

codebook %>%

  select(name, details, labels) %>%
  knitr::kable()

3. Build the Daily Table

What is in a row

Open Play surveys once a day at 2 PM, so each row is already one person on one day (beep is always 1). No aggregation is needed and there is no minimum-prompts rule. The work is recoding and restricting to play days.

table(beep = raw$beep)
## beep
##     1 
## 16346

Clean the diary

16,346 days are kept. The cleaning script does the following:

  • Checkboxes to No/Yes factors, with skip-pattern blanks recoded rather than imputed. The social-play boxes are “No” on days without play. The stress event types are “No” on days without a stressful event.
  • Summaries. The four social-play boxes were summarized into play_context, and the typed platform answers were grouped into platform, each with a “Did not play” level. The rules are listed later in this section.
  • Stress severity (four options) is an ordered factor, and stress_worst is the highest severity that day.
  • Swapped columns fixed. In the source data, the severity ratings for the “health” and “other” events are stored in each other’s columns. The cleaning swaps them back.
  • Type of day. Holiday and vacation day are combined into one level.
  • Dropped:
    • bookkeeping (date, beep, survey_duration, baseline_day, ideal_baseline_day, n_valid, original_wave);
    • the attention-check and duplicate-item columns for the needs scale;
    • free text (most_recent_game, displaced_activity).
# 1. The swapped stress ratings. In the source data the "health" and "other"
# severity ratings sit in each other's columns: every day with the health box
# checked has its rating in how_stressful_other and none in
# how_stressful_health, and the reverse holds for "other". Check this, then
# swap them back. The swap is made on a copy, so raw stays as downloaded.
swap_check <- c(
  health_checked_other_rated = sum(!is.na(raw$stress_events_health) & !is.na(raw$how_stressful_other)),
  health_checked             = sum(!is.na(raw$stress_events_health)),
  other_checked_health_rated = sum(!is.na(raw$stress_events_other) & !is.na(raw$how_stressful_health)),
  other_checked              = sum(!is.na(raw$stress_events_other)))
swap_check
## health_checked_other_rated             health_checked 
##                        531                        531 
## other_checked_health_rated              other_checked 
##                        594                        594
stopifnot(swap_check[1] == swap_check[2], swap_check[3] == swap_check[4])

src <- raw %>%
  rename(how_stressful_health = how_stressful_other,
         how_stressful_other  = how_stressful_health)

# 2. Recode
yes_no <- function(x) factor(x, levels = c("No", "Yes"))

# A checkbox holds its label when checked and NA when not. On days the
# question was not shown (no play, no stress), unchecked means "No".
# `asked` is TRUE when shown, FALSE when skipped by design, and NA when the
# gate question itself is missing.
checkbox <- function(x, asked) {
  factor(ifelse(is.na(asked), NA, ifelse(!is.na(x), "Yes", "No")),
         levels = c("No", "Yes"))
}

social_cols <- c("social_singleplayer", "social_friends_realworld",
                 "social_friends_online", "social_strangers")
event_cols  <- grep("^stress_events_", names(src), value = TRUE)
sev_cols    <- grep("^how_stressful_", names(src), value = TRUE)
sev_levels  <- c("No event", "Not at all", "Not very", "Somewhat", "Very")

daily <- src %>%
  mutate(
    played24hr = yes_no(played24hr),
    had_stress = yes_no(had_stress),

    # who they played with: days without play are "No" for every box; a play
    # day with no box checked is NA (everyone who played, played with someone
    # or alone)
    no_social_box = rowSums(!is.na(across(all_of(social_cols)))) == 0,
    across(all_of(social_cols), ~ checkbox(.x, asked = played24hr == "Yes")),
    across(all_of(social_cols), ~ replace(.x, played24hr == "Yes" & no_social_box, NA)),

    # one summary of the social context, with its own level for non-play days
    play_context = case_when(
      played24hr == "No" ~ "Did not play",
      social_strangers == "Yes" &
        (social_friends_realworld == "Yes" | social_friends_online == "Yes") ~ "Friends + strangers",
      social_strangers == "Yes" ~ "Strangers only",
      social_friends_realworld == "Yes" | social_friends_online == "Yes" ~ "Friends only",
      social_singleplayer == "Yes" ~ "Solo only"),
    play_context = factor(play_context,
                          levels = c("Did not play", "Solo only", "Friends only",
                                     "Friends + strangers", "Strangers only")),

    # platform of the most recent session, grouped; typed "Other" answers
    # (PC, laptop, Chromebook, ...) stay "Other"
    platform = case_when(
      played24hr == "No" ~ "Did not play",
      most_recent_game_plat == "Steam"       ~ "Steam",
      most_recent_game_plat == "Xbox"        ~ "Xbox",
      most_recent_game_plat == "Playstation" ~ "PlayStation",
      grepl("^Nintendo", most_recent_game_plat) ~ "Nintendo",
      most_recent_game_plat %in% c("iOS", "Android", "AMAZON TABLET") ~ "Mobile",
      !is.na(most_recent_game_plat) ~ "Other"),
    platform = factor(platform, levels = c("Did not play", "Steam", "Xbox",
                                           "PlayStation", "Nintendo",
                                           "Mobile", "Other")),

    # stress event types: "No" on days with had_stress = "No"; NA on a "Yes"
    # day with no type checked (the types are unknown)
    any_event_box = rowSums(!is.na(across(all_of(event_cols)))) > 0,
    across(all_of(event_cols), ~ checkbox(.x, asked = had_stress == "Yes")),
    across(all_of(event_cols), ~ replace(.x, had_stress == "Yes" & !any_event_box, NA)),
    n_stress_events = rowSums(across(all_of(event_cols), ~ .x == "Yes")),

    # severity (1 to 4 in the source) as an ordered factor with a "No event"
    # level below "Not at all": four response options, so not numeric
    worst_raw = suppressWarnings(
      do.call(pmax, c(across(all_of(sev_cols)), na.rm = TRUE))),
    across(all_of(sev_cols),
           ~ factor(ifelse(is.na(had_stress), NA, ifelse(is.na(.x), 0, .x)),
                    levels = 0:4, labels = sev_levels, ordered = TRUE)),
    across(all_of(sev_cols), ~ replace(.x, had_stress == "Yes" & !any_event_box, NA)),
    stress_worst = factor(case_when(
      had_stress == "No"  ~ 0,
      had_stress == "Yes" ~ worst_raw),    # NA if "Yes" but nothing rated
      levels = 0:4, labels = sev_levels, ordered = TRUE),

    # type of day: holiday and vacation day (2 to 3% of days each) both mean a
    # weekday off, so they are combined
    day_type = factor(day_type,
                      levels = c("Regular work day", "Regular day off", "Weekend",
                                 "Holiday", "Vacation day", "Other (please specify):"),
                      labels = c("Work day", "Day off", "Weekend",
                                 "Holiday or vacation", "Holiday or vacation", "Other"))
    # numeric items stay numbers: gaming_* and needs_* (1 to 7), sleep_quality
    # (1 to 5), affective_valence and life_satisfaction (0 to 100)
  )

# an event type that was checked must have a severity rating, and only then
for (e in sub("stress_events_", "", event_cols)) {
  sev <- if (e == "home") "how_stressful_home_issue" else paste0("how_stressful_", e)
  stopifnot(all((daily[[paste0("stress_events_", e)]] == "Yes") ==
                  (daily[[sev]] > "No event"), na.rm = TRUE))
}

# 3. Keep the variables, one row per person per day, in id and day order
daily <- daily %>%
  arrange(id, day) %>%
  select(id, day, affective_valence, life_satisfaction, sleep_quality, day_type,
         played24hr, starts_with("gaming_"), all_of(social_cols), play_context, platform,
         starts_with("needs_"),
         had_stress, all_of(event_cols), n_stress_events, all_of(sev_cols), stress_worst)

# the clean table has the same person days as the download
stopifnot(nrow(daily) == nrow(raw),
          setequal(paste(daily$id, daily$day), paste(raw$id, raw$day)))
dim(daily)
## [1] 16346    42

The attention check failed on no day, so dropping it loses nothing:

table(bpnsfs_failed_att_check = raw$bpnsfs_failed_att_check, useNA = "ifany")

What the analysis adds

Added back from the download (joined by id and day):

  • most_recent_game, used once to build the game type (below). It is not a predictor.
  • date, used only for two checks: platform missingness by month (Section 4) and the intake-timing leakage check (Section 7).

Left out of the analysis:

  • Affective valence (“How are you feeling right now?”). It is answered in the same sitting as life satisfaction and is close to the same thing on a given day (correlation below). A model that used it would mostly translate valence into life satisfaction. It is the target in another form.
  • n_stress_events and the seven individual severity ratings. The stress information enters as had_stress, the seven event types, and the worst rating that day.
  • The four social-play checkboxes. They enter through play_context.
  • Lags. Every predictor here is from the same day, so no lags are built.
round(cor(daily$affective_valence, daily$life_satisfaction, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
## [1] 0.87
dat <- daily %>%
  select(-affective_valence, -n_stress_events, -starts_with("how_stressful_")) %>%
  left_join(raw %>% select(id, day, date, most_recent_game), by = c("id", "day"))

stopifnot(nrow(dat) == nrow(daily))
dim(dat)
## [1] 16346    35

Play days only

The six BANGS items are asked only on days the person played in the last 24 hours. Our question is about play days, so the daily table keeps only those days, as the proposal says. Days with a missing answer to the play question are dropped with them.

  filter(played24hr %in% "Yes") %>%
  select(-played24hr) %>%
  mutate(play_context = droplevels(play_context),   # "Did not play" no longer occurs

The 271 days with no answer to the play question are nearly all empty surveys. 248 of them have no life satisfaction rating either, so they could not have been used anyway.

Play days with no gaming answers. On some play days the person said they played, then skipped every gaming question: no title, no social box, no platform, and no BANGS item. These days are dropped:

  • The question is about what a day of gaming was like, and these days say nothing about it. Every gaming predictor would be imputed, so each day would add filled-in values, not information.
  • They would also be miscoded. A blank title is “Unclassified,” and the game-type rules (below) read a missing play context as solo.
bangs <- c("gaming_autonomy", "gaming_wish_else", "gaming_progress",
           "gaming_disappointed", "gaming_relationships", "gaming_toxic")
needs <- c("needs_autonomy_satisfied", "needs_autonomy_frustrated",
           "needs_competence_satisfied", "needs_competence_frustrated",
           "needs_relatedness_satisfied", "needs_relatedness_frustrated")

no_title  <- is.na(dat$most_recent_game) | trimws(dat$most_recent_game) == ""
no_gaming <- no_title & is.na(dat$play_context) & is.na(dat$platform) &
             rowSums(!is.na(dat[bangs])) == 0

no_gaming_n <- c(days = sum(no_gaming),
                 with_target = sum(no_gaming & !is.na(dat$life_satisfaction)))
no_gaming_n
##        days with_target 
##          16           4
dat <- dat[!no_gaming, ]

counts <- rbind(counts, data.frame(step = "Play days with gaming answers",
                                   days = nrow(dat), people = n_distinct(dat$id)))
counts

Ordinal items follow one rule. An item with five or more ordered response options is treated as numeric, and one with fewer is treated as an ordered factor.

  • The BANGS and needs items (1 to 7) and sleep quality (1 to 5) are numeric.
  • The worst-stressor rating has four options, so it is an ordered factor (below).

Type of game

most_recent_game is typed free text. We clean each title (lowercase, accents removed, punctuation stripped) and look up its genre in two files:

  • game_classification.csv, a hand-reviewed list of titles and genres;
  • game_classification_excluded.csv, the titles that were only named on solo days or are single-player games. These were classified by matching patterns in the titles and not reviewed by hand.

Each genre is then coded by who the other people in the game are:

  • single-player;
  • non-competitive (co-op, MMO, sandbox, casual);
  • individual competition;
  • team competition;
  • unknown.

On days with other players (friends, strangers, or both), these rules apply:

  • Games that can be played either solo or in a squad (Fortnite, PUBG, Warzone), Minecraft, and Roblox are coded from who the person played with: with friends, team competition; strangers only, individual competition.
  • Single-player games with a co-op mode count as non-competitive.
  • Titles neither lookup file can classify are “Unknown.”

On solo-only days, the person’s own answer decides. On a solo-only day the person answered “Single-player games only” when asked what kind of social interaction they took part in while gaming. Every game on such a day is coded single-player, whatever its genre in the lookup files. The reasons:

  • The lookup only says what a game can be. Many games coded as competitive or co-op also have modes played alone or against the computer (Call of Duty, Mario Kart, WWE 2K25, Minecraft, Genshin Impact). The person knows which mode they played. The lookup does not.
  • The session items are answered from the person’s own view of the session. The BANGS items (relationships, toxicity, disappointment) ask how the most recent session felt. They have to be read in the context the person reported, not in one we assign from the title.
  • We do not overrule what people said in the survey. Where the person’s description of their gaming day and our classification of the game disagree, the person’s description wins.
  • It also covers titles the lookup cannot classify. The solo-day titles come from the lookup file that was not reviewed by hand, which leaves many single-player games “Unclassified” (Pokémon Shield, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, Civilization). And it removes cases where similar games got different codes (College Football 25 as individual competition, College Football 26 as unclassified).

The table after the chunk shows what the genre rules would have given on the solo-only days.

clean_name <- function(x) {
  x <- iconv(x, from = "UTF-8", to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT", sub = "")
  x <- gsub("[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", tolower(x))
  x <- trimws(gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", x))
  x[is.na(x)] <- ""
  x
}

# the reviewed list comes first, so its genre wins if a title is in both files
lookup_cols  <- c("game", "genre", "classified_by")
genre_lookup <- rbind(
  read.csv(data_path("game_classification.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)[, lookup_cols],
  read.csv(data_path("game_classification_excluded.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)[, lookup_cols])
genre_lookup <- genre_lookup[!duplicated(genre_lookup$game), ]

# a title missing from both files stops the knit rather than being guessed
genre_of <- function(name) {
  genre <- genre_lookup$genre[match(name, genre_lookup$game)]
  if (anyNA(genre)) stop("Not in the lookup files: ",
                         paste(unique(name[is.na(genre)]), collapse = ", "))
  genre
}

# answers that name more than one game; each game is classified on its own
multi_game <- list(
  "baldurs gate 3 echoes of the plum grove" = c("baldurs gate 3", "echoes of the plum grove"),
  "btd 6 roblox"                       = c("btd 6", "roblox"),
  "btd 6 rematch"                      = c("btd 6", "rematch"),
  "btd 6 warframe roblox"              = c("btd 6", "warframe", "roblox"),
  "btd 6 warframe roblox terraria"     = c("btd 6", "warframe", "roblox", "terraria"),
  "dbd roblox"                         = c("dbd", "roblox"),
  "dead by daylight and roblox"        = c("dead by daylight", "roblox"),
  "dune awakening erenshor"            = c("dune awakening", "erenshor"),
  "expedition 33 and fortnite"         = c("expedition 33", "fortnite"),
  "fallout 4 dead by daylight"         = c("fallout 4", "dead by daylight"),
  "fornite and rocket league"          = c("fortnite", "rocket league"),
  "fortnite and avowed"                = c("fortnite", "avowed"),
  "fortnite and battle teams 2"        = c("fortnite", "battle teams 2"),
  "fortnite call of duty"              = c("fortnite", "call of duty"),

  "marvel rivals smurfvillage"         = c("marvel rivals", "smurfs village"),

  "minecraft and marvel rivals"        = c("minecraft", "marvel rivals"),
  "minecraft bf4 nhl 25"               = c("minecraft", "battlefield 4", "nhl"),
  "minecraft roblox"                   = c("minecraft", "roblox"),
  "mix of shcedule 1 and game of thrones" = c("schedule 1", "game of thrones"),
  "nba 2k25 wwe 2k25"                  = c("nba 2k25", "wwe 2k25"),
  "nhl 25 minecraft and battlefield 4" = c("nhl", "minecraft", "battlefield 4"),
  "no man s sky deep rock galactic"    = c("no man s sky", "deep rock galactic"),
  "pokemon go and royal match"         = c("pokemon go", "royal match"),
  "powerwashing simulator club penguin" = c("powerwash simulator", "club penguin"),
  "roblox btd 6"                       = c("roblox", "btd 6"),
  "roblox btd 6 limbus company"        = c("roblox", "btd 6", "limbus company"),
  "roblox btd 6 osrs"                  = c("roblox", "btd 6", "osrs"),
  "roblox fortnite"                    = c("roblox", "fortnite"),
  "sun haven coral island"             = c("sun haven", "coral island"),
  "sun haven echoes of the plum grove" = c("sun haven", "echoes of the plum grove"),
  "the walking dead fortnite"          = c("the walking dead", "fortnite"),
  "word find stud io poker"            = c("word find", "poker"))
code_competition <- function(game_category, play_context) {
  with_friends <- play_context %in% c("Friends only", "Friends + strangers")
  with_others  <- with_friends | play_context %in% "Strangers only"
  case_when(
    game_category == "Solo or co-op" & with_others ~ "Non-competitive",
    game_category == "Solo or co-op" ~ "Single-player",
    game_category == "Competitive team" ~ "Team competition",
    game_category == "Squad or solo" & with_friends ~ "Team competition",
    game_category == "Squad or solo" ~ "Individual competition",
    game_category == "Head-to-head" ~ "Individual competition",
    game_category %in% c("Online co-op / MMO", "Sandbox / social",
                         "Casual / mobile") ~ "Non-competitive",
    game_category %in% c("Minecraft", "Roblox") & with_friends ~ "Team competition",
    game_category %in% c("Minecraft", "Roblox") & with_others ~ "Individual competition",
    game_category %in% c("Minecraft", "Roblox") ~ "Non-competitive",
    game_category == "Mobile (single-player)" ~ "Single-player",
    game_category == "Single-player" ~ "Single-player",
    TRUE ~ "Unknown")
}

# several games named: on days with others, single-player games are dropped;
# if the games left agree the day gets their code, otherwise "Unknown"
combine_games <- function(name, play_context) {
  codes <- unique(code_competition(genre_of(multi_game[[name]]), play_context))
  with_others <- play_context %in% c("Friends only", "Friends + strangers",
                                     "Strangers only")
  if (with_others && any(codes != "Single-player")) {
    codes <- setdiff(codes, "Single-player")
  }
  if (length(codes) == 1) codes else "Unknown"
}

# code_competition() reads a missing play context as solo, so a missing context
# is allowed only on days with no title (no gaming answers at all)
stopifnot(all(clean_name(dat$most_recent_game)[is.na(dat$play_context)] == ""))

dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(game_clean    = clean_name(most_recent_game),
         game_category = genre_of(game_clean),
         game_type     = code_competition(game_category, play_context))

several <- dat$game_category == "Multiple games"
dat$game_type[several] <- mapply(combine_games, dat$game_clean[several],
                                 as.character(dat$play_context[several]))

Of the 5,391 solo-only days, the genre rules alone would have given 899 a competitive or non-competitive code and left 1,068 unknown. The person’s answer codes them all as single-player. Game type and play context now overlap on these days by design, so the importance of the two (Section 9) should be read together.

On days with other players, the most recent game can still be a single-player game (834 days). That is not a contradiction. The play context covers the whole day, while the game type describes the most recent session.

Stress

The stress predictors are:

  • had_stress (“Did anything happen to you in the last 24 hours that most people would consider stressful?”);
  • the seven event types as No/Yes factors;
  • stress_worst, the highest severity rating that day, as an ordered factor.

The coding rules:

  • Event types. “No” on a day the stress question was answered “No.” Missing on a day the stress question itself is missing. Otherwise “Yes” if the box was checked and “No” if not.
  • Worst stressor.
    • “None” if there was no stressful event.
    • Otherwise the highest severity rating, where the scale runs 1 = not at all to 4 = very.
    • Missing if the person said “Yes” but rated no event.
    • It is an ordered factor because the scale has only four options.

The group’s cleaning (above) built these columns with the same rules. The chunk below rebuilds both from the download with the rules above and checks that every play day agrees.

event_cols <- grep("^stress_events_", names(dat), value = TRUE)

# the gate question and the follow-ups agree: every "Yes" has a type checked
table(had_stress = dat$had_stress,
      any_type_yes = rowSums(sapply(dat[event_cols], function(x) x == "Yes")) > 0,
      useNA = "ifany")
##           any_type_yes
## had_stress FALSE  TRUE  <NA>
##       No   10612     0     0
##       Yes      0  1798     0
##       <NA>     0     0     9
# the rules above applied to the download, play days only
raw_play <- raw[match(paste(dat$id, dat$day), paste(raw$id, raw$day)), ]
rule_types <- sapply(event_cols, function(v)
  ifelse(is.na(raw_play$had_stress), NA, ifelse(!is.na(raw_play[[v]]), "Yes", "No")))
sev   <- as.matrix(raw_play[grep("^how_stressful_", names(raw_play))])
worst <- suppressWarnings(apply(sev, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE))
rule_worst <- ifelse(raw_play$had_stress == "No", 0,
                   ifelse(raw_play$had_stress == "Yes" & rowSums(!is.na(sev)) > 0,
                          worst, NA))

# same answers on every play day
stopifnot(identical(unname(rule_types), unname(sapply(dat[event_cols], as.character))))
stopifnot(identical(as.numeric(rule_worst),
                    as.numeric(as.integer(dat$stress_worst) - 1)))   # "No event" = 0

table(rules_above = rule_worst, group_cleaning = dat$stress_worst, useNA = "ifany")
##            group_cleaning
## rules_above No event Not at all Not very Somewhat  Very  <NA>
##        0       10612          0        0        0     0     0
##        1           0          2        0        0     0     0
##        2           0          0      218        0     0     0
##        3           0          0        0      936     0     0
##        4           0          0        0        0   642     0
##        <NA>        0          0        0        0     0     9

The two codings agree on every play day. Two notes on the check:

  • The rule for a “Yes” with no type checked. The group’s cleaning makes the event types missing on such a day, while the rules above code them “No.” The first table above shows that no play day has this pattern, so the two rules give the same data here.
  • The health/other swap. The swap that the cleaning fixes does not change either column used here. The worst rating is the highest across all seven severity columns, whichever column a rating sits in. The event types come from the checkboxes, not the severity columns.

Merging “Not at all” into “Not very.” The worst-stressor factor has four levels: None < Not very < Somewhat < Very. Only 2 play days have “Not at all” as their worst rating. We code those days as “Not very” for three reasons:

  1. Two days cannot support a level of their own. The elastic net would estimate a contrast from two days, which is noise. With ten grouped folds, the level would be missing entirely from most folds’ training or held-out data. The forest’s smallest leaf is five days, so it could never isolate them.
  2. “Not very” is the nearest level. Both mean the event was mild, and the two are neighbors on the ordered scale. Merging neighbors keeps the order that makes the variable ordinal.
  3. “None” would be wrong. The person did report a stressful event, and that day’s event types say so. Coding the worst rating “None” would contradict those columns on the same day.

The cost is negligible: two days out of 12,419.

# shorter names for the event types
dat <- dat %>%
  rename(stress_argument       = stress_events_argument,
         stress_discrimination = stress_events_discrimination,
         stress_friend_family  = stress_events_friend_rel,
         stress_health         = stress_events_health,
         stress_home           = stress_events_home,
         stress_other          = stress_events_other,
         stress_work_school    = stress_events_work_school)

stress_types <- c("stress_argument", "stress_discrimination",
                  "stress_friend_family", "stress_health", "stress_home",
                  "stress_work_school", "stress_other")

# four levels; the duplicated label merges "Not at all" into "Not very"
dat$stress_worst <- factor(as.character(dat$stress_worst),
                           levels = c("No event", "Not at all", "Not very",
                                      "Somewhat", "Very"),
                           labels = c("None", "Not very", "Not very",
                                      "Somewhat", "Very"),
                           ordered = TRUE)

table(dat$stress_worst, useNA = "always")
## 
##     None Not very Somewhat     Very     <NA> 
##    10612      220      936      642        9
# share of play days with each kind of event
sapply(dat[stress_types], function(x) round(100 * mean(x == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE), 1))

Person characteristics from the intake survey

The intake survey came before the diary. The demographics are coded as follows:

  • Age is in years.
  • Gender is man, woman, or non-binary / gender diverse. Typed answers are coded by the identity they state.
  • Employment is full-time, part-time or self-employed, student, or not employed.
  • Education is the highest level completed, numeric 1 to 6 (six ordered levels).
  • Relationship status is single, partnered, or divorced / separated / widowed.
  • Cares for children is yes if that caregiving box was checked, and no if the person answered the question without checking it.

“Prefer not to say” is a non-answer and becomes missing (Section 4).

blank_na <- function(x) { x <- trimws(x); x[x == ""] <- NA; x }

emp <- tolower(blank_na(intake$employment))
ms  <- tolower(blank_na(intake$marital_status))
edu <- blank_na(intake$edu_level)

care_cols <- c("care_children", "care_elderly", "care_disability",
               "care_none", "care_other")
answered_care <- rowSums(!is.na(intake[care_cols]) & intake[care_cols] != "") > 0

person <- data.frame(
  id  = intake$pid,
  age = intake$age,
  gender = case_when(
    intake$gender %in% c("Man", "Transgender Man", "Transgender Man (FTM)") ~ "Man",
    intake$gender %in% c("Woman", "trans woman") ~ "Woman",
    intake$gender == "Prefer not to say" | is.na(blank_na(intake$gender)) ~ NA_character_,
    TRUE ~ "Non-binary / gender diverse"),
  employment = case_when(
    is.na(emp) | grepl("prefer not", emp)              ~ NA_character_,
    grepl("student", emp)                               ~ "Student",
    emp %in% c("working full-time", "military")         ~ "Full-time",
    emp == "working part-time" |
      grepl("self|freelanc|gig|streamer|prolific", emp) ~ "Part-time / self-employed",
    TRUE                                                ~ "Not employed"),
  education = case_when(
    edu %in% c("Less than a high school diploma or equivalent",
               "Completed Primary School")                    ~ 1,
    edu %in% c("High school graduate or equivalent",
               "Completed Secondary School")                  ~ 2,
    edu %in% c("Some college but no degree",
               "Some University but no degree",
               "Vocational or Similar")                       ~ 3,
    edu == "Associate degree"                                 ~ 4,
    edu %in% c("Bachelor's degree", "University Bachelors Degree") ~ 5,
    edu %in% c("Master's degree, professional degree, or doctoral degree",
               "Graduate or professional degree (MA, MS, MBA, PhD, etc)") ~ 6,
    TRUE                                                      ~ NA_real_),
  relationship = case_when(
    is.na(ms) | ms == "prefer not to say"                     ~ NA_character_,
    ms == "single, never married"                             ~ "Single",
    grepl("divorc|widow|^separated", ms)                      ~ "Divorced / separated / widowed",
    grepl("married|partner|engaged|relationship|living with|civil union", ms) ~ "Partnered",
    TRUE                                                      ~ NA_character_),
  cares_for_children = case_when(
    !is.na(intake$care_children) & intake$care_children != "" ~ "Yes",
    answered_care                                             ~ "No",
    TRUE                                                      ~ NA_character_),
  intake_date = intake$date,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  filter(id %in% dat$id)

# one intake record per person, so the join cannot duplicate days
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(person$id))

id, day, date, and intake_date are kept only to split by person and to check leakage. They are removed before any model sees the data.

4. Missing Data

Why are they missing?

Platform is the only daily variable with substantial missingness. It is missing almost entirely in the first months of the study, which suggests the question was added to the survey partway through:

days %>%
  mutate(month = format(date, "%Y-%m")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(days = n(),
            pct_platform_missing = round(100 * mean(is.na(platform)), 1),
            mean_life_sat = round(mean(life_satisfaction, na.rm = TRUE), 1))
month days pct_platform_missing mean_life_sat
2024-10 198 100.0 62.8
2025-02 386 74.6 67.2
2025-03 956 10.0 65.8
2025-04 3512 2.6 65.1
2025-05 192 1.6 74.8
2025-06 2448 0.8 66.0
2025-07 4088 1.1 66.7
2025-08 639 0.8 67.2 
platform_target <- days %>%
  group_by(platform_missing = is.na(platform)) %>%
  summarise(days = n(),
            mean_life_sat = round(mean(life_satisfaction, na.rm = TRUE), 1))
platform_target
platform_missing days mean_life_sat
FALSE 11672 66.1
TRUE 747 67.3

Missing platform depends on when someone took part, which is an observed fact, and not on their life satisfaction. Mean life satisfaction is 67.3 on days with platform missing and 66.1 on days with it recorded, so the gap does not mark a different kind of day. So it is most likely MAR, and KNN imputation inside the recipe fits that mechanism.

# missing platform days, by whether the person gave a platform on other days
platform_gap <- days %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(answered_other_days = any(!is.na(platform))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(is.na(platform)) %>%
  count(answered_other_days)
platform_gap
answered_other_days n
FALSE 266
TRUE 481 
# share of each person's answered days on their usual platform
# (people with 5 or more answered days)
usual_platform <- days %>%
  filter(!is.na(platform)) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  filter(n() >= 5) %>%
  summarise(share = max(table(platform)) / n())
round(mean(usual_platform$share), 2)
## [1] 0.77

A limitation. KNN fills each missing platform from similar days of other people. It does not look at the person’s own answers on other days. 481 of the 747 missing days belong to people who gave a platform on other days, and people played on their usual platform on 77% of their days. For those days, the person’s usual platform would likely be a better guess. We keep KNN, so that platform is imputed like every other predictor.

The intake variables are missing for two reasons:

  • The person has no intake record. The most likely cause is a gap in linking the two surveys, which would be close to MCAR.
  • The person chose “Prefer not to say.” This could be MNAR, because someone may decline a question because of their answer.
# people in the daily table, by why each intake answer is missing
said_prefer_not <- function(answers) grepl("prefer not", tolower(answers))
in_person <- match(person$id, intake$pid)
care_prefer_not <- !is.na(intake$care_prefer_not_say[in_person]) &
                   intake$care_prefer_not_say[in_person] != ""

intake_missing <- data.frame(
  variable         = person_preds,
  no_intake_record = n_distinct(days$id[!days$id %in% intake$pid]),
  declined         = c(age          = 0,
                       gender       = sum(said_prefer_not(intake$gender[in_person])),
                       employment   = sum(said_prefer_not(intake$employment[in_person])),
                       education    = sum(said_prefer_not(intake$edu_level[in_person])),
                       relationship = sum(said_prefer_not(intake$marital_status[in_person])),
                       cares_for_children = sum(is.na(person$cares_for_children) & care_prefer_not)),
  row.names = NULL)
# an intake record, no answer, and no "Prefer not to say": the question was skipped
intake_missing$skipped <- colSums(is.na(person[person_preds])) - intake_missing$declined
stopifnot(intake_missing$skipped >= 0)
intake_missing
variable no_intake_record declined skipped
age 46 0 0
gender 46 1 0
employment 46 1 1
education 46 3 0
relationship 46 9 0
cares_for_children 46 12 0

Most missing intake values come from the 46 people with no intake record. Only 1 to 12 people declined or skipped any one question, so the part that could be MNAR is small.

So the categorical intake variables get their own “Not reported” level instead of being imputed. Age and education are filled with the training median inside the recipe. Both are person-level facts, so every day of a person gets the same value, which KNN would not guarantee. For the people with no intake record, the “Not reported” levels already mark them as missing, so the median does not hide that. Only the 3 people who declined the education question are filled without such a marker.

daily_vars <- c(bangs, needs, "sleep_quality", "day_type", "play_context",
                "had_stress", stress_types, "stress_worst")
max_daily_missing <- max(miss_table$n_missing[miss_table$variable %in% daily_vars])

# each block is missing all at once: 0 or 6 items on every day
table(bangs_missing = rowSums(is.na(days[bangs])))
## bangs_missing
##     0     6 
## 12409    10
table(needs_missing = rowSums(is.na(days[needs])))
## needs_missing
##     0     6 
## 12408    11

The daily items (the BANGS items, the needs items, sleep, stress, type of day, play context) are each missing on 11 play days or fewer (0.1%). A day missing one BANGS item is missing all six, and the same holds for the needs items. These are unfinished surveys. Leaving a survey unfinished is unlikely to depend on the answers never given, so these are close to MCAR. They are imputed with KNN inside the recipe. KNN fills each column on its own, so on an imputed day the stress columns may not agree with each other (for example, had_stress “No” with an event type “Yes”). This can happen on at most 9 days.

The worst stressor would also be missing on a day the person said “Yes” but rated no event. 0 play days have that pattern, so it is missing only when the stress question itself is missing.

Decisions

c(missing_target = sum(is.na(days$life_satisfaction)))
## missing_target 
##             12
days <- days %>% filter(!is.na(life_satisfaction))

counts <- rbind(counts, data.frame(step = "Play days with a target",
                                   days = nrow(days), people = n_distinct(days$id)))
counts
step days people
All diary days 16346 1284
Play days 12435 1171
Play days with gaming answers 12419 1170
Play days with a target 12407 1169 
# days complete on every predictor, counted before the "Not reported" levels
# are added (afterwards those days would look complete)
c(complete_days = sum(complete.cases(days[model_vars])))
## complete_days 
##         11353
not_reported <- function(x) {
  factor(ifelse(is.na(x), "Not reported", as.character(x)),
         levels = c(levels(x), "Not reported"))
}
for (v in c("gender", "employment", "relationship", "cares_for_children")) {
  days[[v]] <- not_reported(days[[v]])
}

sapply(days[c("gender", "employment", "relationship", "cares_for_children")], table)

Summary: how each kind of missing value is handled.

What is missing Variables Handling Where and when Why
Question skipped by design social boxes on non-play days; stress types and severity when had_stress is No Recoded to “No” / “No event”, not imputed Cleaning (Section 3) The answer is known from the skip pattern
The play question played24hr Day dropped Section 3 Cannot tell whether it is a play day; nearly all are empty surveys
Every gaming answer on a play day title, social boxes, platform, and all BANGS items Day dropped Section 3 The day says nothing about the session
The target life_satisfaction Day dropped Section 4, before the split Nothing to train on or score
An unreadable or conflicting game title game_type “Unknown” level Section 3 A real category of answer, not a gap
A categorical intake answer gender, employment, relationship, cares for children “Not reported” level Section 4, before the split Declining may depend on the answer (MNAR); the level keeps that information
A numeric intake answer age, education Training median Model recipes (Section 8), relearned in each fold A fact about the person, so every day of a person gets the same value
A daily answer, in the models BANGS items, needs items (set A), sleep, type of day, platform, had_stress, stress types, stress_worst KNN, 5 neighbors, from the other predictors (never the target) Model recipes (Section 8), relearned in each fold Unfinished surveys (MCAR) and the late-added platform question (MAR)
A BANGS or needs block, before clustering and PCA the 6 BANGS items, the 6 needs items Training median Block recipes (Section 6), learned once on the training days The blocks must be filled first, and a day missing one item misses all six, so KNN has nothing to match on
Cluster and component scores play_day_type, need_satisfaction, need_frustration Nothing missing Section 6 Built from the already-filled blocks

5. Split by Person

days_per_person <- table(days$id)
summary(as.vector(days_per_person))
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    1.00    2.00    7.00   10.61   19.00   30.00
# share of life satisfaction variance between people (one-way ANOVA ICC)
aov_fit <- anova(lm(life_satisfaction ~ factor(id), data = days))
ms_b  <- aov_fit["factor(id)", "Mean Sq"]
ms_w  <- aov_fit["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
k_avg <- (nrow(days) - sum(days_per_person^2) / nrow(days)) / (length(days_per_person) - 1)
icc   <- (ms_b - ms_w) / (ms_b + (k_avg - 1) * ms_w)
round(icc, 2)
## [1] 0.73

About 73% of the variation in daily life satisfaction lies between people. The intake predictors are also constant within a person. A split over days would put most people in both sets. A model could then learn each person’s usual level from their training days, partly through the intake variables, and score well on the test set without predicting anything new.

So we depart from the handout’s day-level initial_split(), as the proposal says, and split by person:

  • group_initial_split() puts 70% of people in the training set and 30% in the test set, with seed 559.
  • The split is stratified on each person’s mean life satisfaction (quartiles). This is the person-level version of “stratified on the target.”
  • Cross-validation also holds out whole people.

The test set therefore checks how well the model does for new players.

person_ls <- tapply(days$life_satisfaction, days$id, mean)
days$ls_strata <- cut(person_ls[as.character(days$id)],
                      breaks = quantile(person_ls, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25)),
                      include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)

set.seed(559)
split <- group_initial_split(days, group = id, prop = 0.7, strata = ls_strata)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

split_sizes <- data.frame(
  set    = c("training", "test"),
  days   = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  people = c(n_distinct(train$id), n_distinct(test$id)),
  mean_life_sat = round(c(mean(train$life_satisfaction), mean(test$life_satisfaction)), 1),
  sd_life_sat   = round(c(sd(train$life_satisfaction), sd(test$life_satisfaction)), 1))
split_sizes
set days people mean_life_sat sd_life_sat
training 8677 814 65.7 24.2
test 3730 355 67.2 22.4 
# no person is in both sets
length(intersect(train$id, test$id))
## [1] 0

From here on, test is used only to receive the cluster labels and component scores learned on train, until the final evaluation in Section 9.

n_folds <- 10

set.seed(559)
folds <- groupKFold(train$id, k = n_folds)

# The folds are fit in parallel (Section 8), so set.seed() alone would not
# fix the random parts of each fit (the forests' bootstrap samples).
# caret takes one seed per fold and tuning value, plus one for the final fit.
# 1000 per fold covers every tuning grid used here.
fold_seeds <- c(lapply(seq_len(n_folds), function(i) sample.int(1e6, 1000)),
                list(sample.int(1e6, 1)))
ctrl  <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = n_folds, index = folds,
                      savePredictions = "final", seeds = fold_seeds)

# people and days held out in each fold
sapply(folds, function(rows) c(people_out = n_distinct(train$id[-rows]),
                               days_out   = nrow(train) - length(rows)))
##            Fold01 Fold02 Fold03 Fold04 Fold05 Fold06 Fold07 Fold08 Fold09
## people_out     72     82     98     76     86     81     71    100     83
## days_out      777    980    938    870   1037    704    725    985    912
##            Fold10
## people_out     65
## days_out      749

The handout asks us to state the number of folds. We use 10 grouped folds, the number the handout asks for in the report (“use ten in your report”). Each fold holds out about a tenth of the training people. All models (Section 8) get these same folds through index.

6. Unsupervised Analysis

Everything in this section is fit on the training days only. Test days get their cluster labels and component scores from the training fit. Neither block contains the target. Both are imputed (training medians) and centered and scaled (training means and SDs) in a recipe first, because K-means and PCA work from distances and cannot take missing values. Both blocks are 1 to 7 numeric items, so there are no categorical items to encode.

Why the blocks are filled with the median here, but with KNN in the models.

  • The blocks must be filled first. K-means and PCA cannot run with missing values, and they are run once, here, before any model.
  • KNN has nothing to work with inside a block. KNN fills a missing answer by finding days with similar answers to the other questions. But a day missing one item of a block is missing all six (Section 4), so within the block there are no other answers to compare. The training median is the simple fill that is left.
  • The models are different. Their recipes (Section 8) see every predictor, so KNN has plenty to match on there, and caret relearns it in each fold.
  • No leakage. The medians come from the training days only and never use the target.
  • Small cost. Every filled day gets the same values: the same play-day type and the same two component scores (shown below). Only 1 training and 2 test days are filled for the BANGS items, and 3 training and 0 test days for the needs items. The effect on the structure and on set B is negligible.

6a. Clustering: types of play days

The handout asks for clusters that are types of days. Each play day is clustered on its six BANGS answers, which describe how that day’s most recent gaming session went, so each type is a kind of play day defined by its gaming. Days without play have no BANGS answers and no type.

The block

rec_bangs <- recipe(~ ., data = train[bangs]) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  prep()

train_bangs <- bake(rec_bangs, new_data = train)
test_bangs  <- bake(rec_bangs, new_data = test)

round(cor(train_bangs), 2)
##                      gaming_autonomy gaming_wish_else gaming_progress
## gaming_autonomy                 1.00            -0.41            0.49
## gaming_wish_else               -0.41             1.00           -0.35
## gaming_progress                 0.49            -0.35            1.00
## gaming_disappointed            -0.45             0.41           -0.42
## gaming_relationships            0.19            -0.13            0.25
## gaming_toxic                   -0.26             0.33           -0.23
##                      gaming_disappointed gaming_relationships gaming_toxic
## gaming_autonomy                    -0.45                 0.19        -0.26
## gaming_wish_else                    0.41                -0.13         0.33
## gaming_progress                    -0.42                 0.25        -0.23
## gaming_disappointed                 1.00                -0.09         0.37
## gaming_relationships               -0.09                 1.00         0.05
## gaming_toxic                        0.37                 0.05         1.00

Autonomy and progress go together, and wishing to do something else, disappointment, and toxicity go together. Forming relationships is nearly independent of the rest.

How many types?

We use two criteria: the elbow in the total within-cluster sum of squares, and the average silhouette width. Each K-means fit uses 25 random starts. The silhouette is computed from the distances between all training days.

k_range <- 1:8

km_fits <- lapply(k_range, function(k) {
  set.seed(559)
  kmeans(train_bangs, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
})

bangs_dist <- dist(train_bangs)
k_choice <- data.frame(
  K   = k_range,
  wss = sapply(km_fits, `[[`, "tot.withinss"),
  silhouette = c(NA, sapply(km_fits[-1], function(km)
    mean(silhouette(km$cluster, bangs_dist)[, 3]))))
rm(bangs_dist)

k_choice %>% mutate(share_of_k1 = round(wss / wss[1], 3),
                    silhouette  = round(silhouette, 3))
K wss silhouette share_of_k1
1 52056.00 NA 1.000
2 37276.05 0.292 0.716
3 32298.41 0.218 0.620
4 29119.64 0.211 0.559
5 26640.52 0.210 0.512
6 24769.27 0.210 0.476
7 23352.40 0.210 0.449
8 22107.37 0.199 0.425 
ggplot(k_choice, aes(K, wss)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_range) +
  labs(y = "Total within-cluster sum of squares")

Elbow plot: total within-cluster sum of squares by K (training days). 

ggplot(filter(k_choice, K > 1), aes(K, silhouette)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_range) +
  labs(y = "Average silhouette width")

Average silhouette width by K (training days).

Choosing K. Both criteria point to the same region, and neither gives a sharp answer:

  • The silhouette is highest at K = 2 (0.29). It is 0.22 at K = 3 and stays near that value for every larger K. Silhouettes around 0.2 to 0.3 mean the types overlap. Play days vary continuously and do not fall into separate groups.
  • The elbow bends at K = 2 to 3. Going from 1 to 2 clusters removes 28% of the within-cluster variation, 2 to 3 removes another 10%, and later steps remove less.

We keep K = 3:

  • Against K = 2. K = 2 only separates good play days from bad ones. K = 3 splits the good days by whether the person formed relationships while playing. That is the one BANGS item the others do not capture (the correlation table above), and the split matters for the target (below).
  • Against K = 4. K = 4 is a finer cut. It splits the frustrating days further, but its silhouette is no better and the solution is less stable.
  • Section 8 checks K = 2 and K = 4 against K = 3 on the training folds: profiles, stability, and prediction.
k_final <- 3
km <- km_fits[[k_final]]

km$size
## [1] 3986 2654 2037
round(km$betweenss / km$totss, 2)   # share of variation between the clusters
## [1] 0.38

Profiles and names

The centroids are in z scores. The profile table gives the item means in the original 1 to 7 units, the cluster sizes, and who the person played with.

cluster_profile <- function(labels) {
  train[bangs] %>%
    mutate(cluster = labels) %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>%
    summarise(across(everything(), ~ round(mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), 1)),
              days = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    as.data.frame()
}

cluster_profile(km_fits[[2]]$cluster)   # K = 2, for comparison
cluster gaming_autonomy gaming_wish_else gaming_progress gaming_disappointed gaming_relationships gaming_toxic days
1 6.2 1.7 6.0 1.6 4.0 1.5 5600
2 4.6 3.6 4.3 3.5 3.3 3.0 3077 
cluster_profile(km$cluster)
cluster gaming_autonomy gaming_wish_else gaming_progress gaming_disappointed gaming_relationships gaming_toxic days
1 6.2 1.7 6.0 1.7 5.1 1.7 3986
2 4.6 3.7 4.3 3.7 3.4 3.2 2654
3 6.0 1.9 5.6 1.7 1.5 1.3 2037

The names are assigned by rule, so they stay attached to the right cluster even if the cluster numbers change:

  • the cluster with the highest relationships mean is the connected play day;
  • of the other two, the one with lower autonomy is the frustrating play day;
  • the last is the smooth solo play day.
prof <- cluster_profile(km$cluster)
connected   <- prof$cluster[which.max(prof$gaming_relationships)]
others      <- setdiff(prof$cluster, connected)
frustrating <- others[which.min(prof$gaming_autonomy[match(others, prof$cluster)])]
smooth      <- setdiff(others, c(frustrating))

cluster_names <- character(k_final)
cluster_names[connected]   <- "Connected play day"
cluster_names[frustrating] <- "Frustrating play day"
cluster_names[smooth]      <- "Smooth solo play day"

type_levels <- c("Smooth solo play day", "Connected play day", "Frustrating play day")
train$play_day_type <- factor(cluster_names[km$cluster], levels = type_levels)

table(train$play_day_type)
## 
## Smooth solo play day   Connected play day Frustrating play day 
##                 2037                 3986                 2654
as.data.frame(km$centers) %>%
  mutate(cluster = paste0(cluster_names, " (n = ", km$size, ")")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "item", values_to = "z") %>%
  mutate(item = sub("gaming_", "", item)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(item, z, fill = item)) +
  geom_col() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster) + coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cluster mean (z score)")

Cluster centroids on the six BANGS items (z scores, training days).

Who people played with, and what they played, in each type (row percentages, training days):

round(100 * prop.table(table(train$play_day_type, train$play_context), 1))
##                       
##                        Solo only Friends only Friends + strangers
##   Smooth solo play day        61           11                   6
##   Connected play day          41           33                  12
##   Frustrating play day        36           27                  12
##                       
##                        Strangers only
##   Smooth solo play day             23
##   Connected play day               13
##   Frustrating play day             26
round(100 * prop.table(table(train$play_day_type, train$game_type), 1))
##                       
##                        Single-player Non-competitive Individual competition
##   Smooth solo play day            68              14                      8
##   Connected play day              48              27                      8
##   Frustrating play day            41              17                     10
##                       
##                        Team competition Unknown
##   Smooth solo play day                9       0
##   Connected play day                 17       0
##   Frustrating play day               31       0

What the three types are:

  • Smooth solo play day. The person played the way they wanted and made progress. There was little disappointment and almost no toxicity, but no relationships were formed. Most of these days were solo, single-player play.
  • Connected play day. The gaming went just as smoothly, and the person also formed relationships with other players or characters. These days are split between solo and friends play. The item asks about players or characters, so a story game can count.
  • Frustrating play day. Autonomy and progress were lower, and wishing to do something else, disappointment, and toxicity were higher. Team competition and strangers-only play are more common than on the other types of day.

Compared with the proposal: the expected day with a “satisfying solo session” appears. The days with a “toxic competitive” or “low improvement” session appear together as one frustrating type, which leans toward competitive play but is not defined by it. Toxicity is only moderate even there (mean 3.2 on the 1 to 7 scale, below the midpoint). At K = 4 the two separate (Section 8), but the extra split is less stable and is not supported by the silhouette.

Life satisfaction across the types (training days)

train %>%
  group_by(play_day_type) %>%
  summarise(days = n(),
            mean_life_sat = round(mean(life_satisfaction), 1),
            sd_life_sat   = round(sd(life_satisfaction), 1),
            pct_stress    = round(100 * mean(had_stress == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_sleep    = round(mean(sleep_quality, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
play_day_type days mean_life_sat sd_life_sat pct_stress mean_sleep
Smooth solo play day 2037 65.3 25.2 13.3 3.27
Connected play day 3986 72.7 21.3 11.3 3.45
Frustrating play day 2654 55.5 23.9 18.2 3.01 
ggplot(train, aes(play_day_type, life_satisfaction, fill = play_day_type)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life satisfaction today (0 to 100)")

Life satisfaction by type of play day (training days).

The type of play day is clearly related to life satisfaction that day, even though no BANGS item asks about life. Frustrating play days are the lowest and connected play days the highest. The spread within each type is wide, and these are same-day associations. A bad day may make the gaming feel worse as much as the other way around.

Test days

kmeans() has no predict() method. A test day joins the training centroid it is closest to, in the training-standardized units.

nearest_centroid <- function(x, centers) {
  x  <- as.matrix(x)
  d2 <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(centers)), function(k)
    rowSums((x - matrix(centers[k, ], nrow(x), ncol(x), byrow = TRUE))^2))
  max.col(-d2, ties.method = "first")
}

test$play_day_type <- factor(cluster_names[nearest_centroid(test_bangs, km$centers)],
                            levels = type_levels)

# the rule gives the training days their own clusters back
mean(nearest_centroid(train_bangs, km$centers) == km$cluster)
## [1] 1
round(rbind(train = prop.table(table(train$play_day_type)),
            test  = prop.table(table(test$play_day_type))), 2)
##       Smooth solo play day Connected play day Frustrating play day
## train                 0.23               0.46                 0.31
## test                  0.23               0.46                 0.31
# days with no BANGS answers were filled with the training medians, so they
# all get the play-day type nearest the median profile
table(filled_day_type = c(
  as.character(train$play_day_type[rowSums(is.na(train[bangs])) > 0]),
  as.character(test$play_day_type[rowSums(is.na(test[bangs])) > 0])))
## filled_day_type
## Connected play day

6b. Principal components: dimensions of a day’s needs

The block

rec_needs <- recipe(~ ., data = train[needs]) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  prep()

train_needs <- bake(rec_needs, new_data = train)
test_needs  <- bake(rec_needs, new_data = test)
