pca <- prcomp(train_needs, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)
## Importance of components:
##                           PC1    PC2     PC3     PC4     PC5     PC6
## Standard deviation     1.8758 0.8855 0.75960 0.73585 0.58235 0.48946
## Proportion of Variance 0.5864 0.1307 0.09617 0.09025 0.05652 0.03993
## Cumulative Proportion  0.5864 0.7171 0.81330 0.90355 0.96007 1.00000

How many components?

We use the three rules from the PCA lecture, parallel analysis (one of the criteria the handout lists), and theory:

  • The scree plot. Keep the components before the curve flattens.
  • The eigenvalue rule. A component’s eigenvalue is its variance. Each standardized item has a variance of 1, so a component with an eigenvalue of 1 or more explains more than a single item does. The lecture uses 1 as the cutoff and the walkthrough’s code uses 0.75, so both are shown.
  • Cumulative variance. Keep enough components to explain 80% of the variance.
  • Parallel analysis. Run PCA on 100 sets of random, uncorrelated data of the same size (8677 days by 6 items). Keep a component only if its eigenvalue beats the 95th percentile of the random eigenvalues at the same position, so it holds more than chance alone would give.
  • Theory. What the items were written to measure.
eig <- pca$sdev^2
pve <- eig / sum(eig)

# parallel analysis: eigenvalues of random data with the same rows and columns
set.seed(559)
random_eig <- replicate(100, prcomp(matrix(rnorm(nrow(train_needs) * length(needs)),
                                           ncol = length(needs)), scale. = TRUE)$sdev^2)
pa_cut <- apply(random_eig, 1, quantile, 0.95)

n_comp_rules <- data.frame(PC = seq_along(eig), eigenvalue = round(eig, 2),
                           pve = round(pve, 3), cumulative = round(cumsum(pve), 3),
                           random_95 = round(pa_cut, 3))
n_comp_rules
PC eigenvalue pve cumulative random_95
1 3.52 0.586 0.586 1.048
2 0.78 0.131 0.717 1.026
3 0.58 0.096 0.813 1.015
4 0.54 0.090 0.904 1.001
5 0.34 0.057 0.960 0.990
6 0.24 0.040 1.000 0.977 
# components each rule keeps (eigenvalues fall in order, so a count works)
c(eigenvalue_1      = sum(eig >= 1),
  eigenvalue_0.75   = sum(eig >= 0.75),
  cumulative_80     = which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.80)[1],
  parallel_analysis = sum(eig > pa_cut))
##      eigenvalue_1   eigenvalue_0.75     cumulative_80 parallel_analysis 
##                 1                 2                 3                 1
ggplot(n_comp_rules, aes(PC, pve)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = random_95 / length(needs)), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(eig)) +
  labs(y = "Proportion of variance explained")

Scree plot: proportion of variance explained by each component of the six needs items (training days). The dashed line is the parallel-analysis cutoff on the same scale.

Choosing the number. The rules disagree, which the lecture notes is normal:

Rule Components kept
Scree plot 1: the curve drops steeply from component 1 to 2 (58.6% to 13.1%) and flattens after that
Eigenvalue of 1 or more (lecture) 1
Eigenvalue of 0.75 or more (walkthrough) 2 (the second eigenvalue is 0.78)
80% of the variance 3 (two components explain 71.7%, three 81.3%)
Parallel analysis 1 (the second eigenvalue, 0.78, is below the random cutoff of 1.03)
Theory (self-determination theory) 2: need satisfaction and need frustration

Parallel analysis and the eigenvalue rule at 1 agree here, and with this much data they are close to the same test, so they count as one piece of evidence rather than two. Parallel analysis replaces the fixed cutoff of 1 with the eigenvalues of random data, which stray from 1 only by chance. With 8677 days and 6 items they barely stray (the cutoff for the second component is 1.03). The two rules part ways only when the sample is small or the items are many.

  • The case for one. The first component alone explains 59% of the variance. It is a general “good day for my needs” dimension, with every satisfaction item positive and every frustration item negative.
  • We keep two, as theory and the walkthrough’s cutoff say. Self-determination theory treats satisfaction and frustration as separate experiences, and the proposal predicted exactly these two dimensions. Two components also carry more of the frustration items, which the first component carries less well.
  • Section 8 checks one and three components (the 80% rule’s choice) against two on the training folds.
n_keep <- 2

loadings <- pca$rotation[, 1:n_keep] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:n_keep])
colnames(loadings) <- paste0("PC", 1:n_keep)
round(loadings, 2)
##                                PC1   PC2
## needs_autonomy_satisfied      0.83 -0.34
## needs_autonomy_frustrated    -0.66 -0.53
## needs_competence_satisfied    0.83 -0.34
## needs_competence_frustrated  -0.78 -0.21
## needs_relatedness_satisfied   0.75 -0.29
## needs_relatedness_frustrated -0.73 -0.37

Rotation and names

The unrotated pair is one general component plus a contrast, which is hard to name. A varimax rotation turns the two axes within the same plane. The variance they explain together does not change.

rotation <- varimax(loadings)
rotated  <- unclass(rotation$loadings)
colnames(rotated) <- paste0("RC", 1:n_keep)

# flip each component so its strongest items load positively
flip <- sign(apply(rotated, 2, function(l) l[which.max(abs(l))]))
rotated <- sweep(rotated, 2, flip, "*")

# name each component by which kind of item it carries
sat_items  <- grepl("_satisfied$", rownames(rotated))
is_sat     <- colMeans(abs(rotated[sat_items, ])) > colMeans(abs(rotated[!sat_items, ]))
comp_names <- unname(ifelse(is_sat, "need_satisfaction", "need_frustration"))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(comp_names))
colnames(rotated) <- comp_names

round(rotated, 2)
##                              need_satisfaction need_frustration
## needs_autonomy_satisfied                  0.86            -0.28
## needs_autonomy_frustrated                -0.15             0.83
## needs_competence_satisfied                0.85            -0.28
## needs_competence_frustrated              -0.46             0.67
## needs_relatedness_satisfied               0.76            -0.27
## needs_relatedness_frustrated             -0.31             0.76
# variance explained by the two rotated components together
round(sum(rotated^2) / length(needs), 3)
## [1] 0.717
as.data.frame(rotated) %>%
  mutate(item = factor(sub("needs_", "", rownames(rotated)),
                       levels = rev(sub("needs_", "", rownames(rotated))))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-item, names_to = "component", values_to = "loading") %>%
  ggplot(aes(component, item, fill = loading)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", loading)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

Rotated loadings of the six needs items on the two components.

  • Need satisfaction. The three satisfaction items (autonomy, competence, relatedness) load highly. A high score is a day the person did what they valued, did it well, and felt close to people.
  • Need frustration. The three frustration items load highly (after the flip). A high score is a day the person felt forced, insecure, or excluded. Competence frustration loads on both components.

Compared with the proposal

The proposal expected two components, one for general satisfaction and one for general frustration, rather than one for each need. It read that result as days differing “more in how fulfilling or frustrating they are overall rather than in which specific need is met.” Two numbers help check that reading: how strongly the satisfied and frustrated items go together, and what a third component would hold.

needs_cor <- cor(train_needs)
sat <- grepl("_satisfied$", needs)

# correlations between each satisfied item and each frustrated item
round(range(needs_cor[sat, !sat]), 2)
## [1] -0.59 -0.36
# three varimax-rotated components; the one that carries relatedness
# frustration most, flipped so that item loads positively (Section 8 tests
# whether a third component helps prediction)
L3 <- unclass(varimax(pca$rotation[, 1:3] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:3]))$loadings)
rel_comp <- which.max(abs(L3["needs_relatedness_frustrated", ]))
third <- L3[, rel_comp] * sign(L3["needs_relatedness_frustrated", rel_comp])
round(third, 2)
##     needs_autonomy_satisfied    needs_autonomy_frustrated 
##                        -0.18                         0.16 
##   needs_competence_satisfied  needs_competence_frustrated 
##                        -0.16                         0.37 
##  needs_relatedness_satisfied needs_relatedness_frustrated 
##                        -0.61                         0.85
  • What matches. The two rotated components are need satisfaction and need frustration, as predicted. Each item loads mainly on its own side, and neither component belongs to a single need.
  • Satisfaction and frustration go together. The first unrotated component alone explains 59% of the variance, and every satisfied item correlates between -0.59 and -0.36 with every frustrated item. A day that meets a person’s needs is usually also a day low in frustration. The two rotated scores are uncorrelated only because varimax keeps the axes at right angles. That is a property of the method, not a finding.
  • One need partly stands apart: relatedness. A third component, the one the 80% rule would keep, is mostly relatedness: relatedness frustration loads 0.85 and relatedness satisfaction -0.61. It is small (eigenvalue 0.58, 9.6% of the variance), and Section 8 shows it adds nothing to predicting life satisfaction. Autonomy and competence cannot be told apart: their satisfaction items correlate 0.75.
  • Days and people. The components are fit on days pooled across people, so they mix differences between people with differences between one person’s days. A high need-satisfaction score marks a good day partly because it marks a person whose days usually go well.

The proposal’s reading holds, with one qualification: the days differ mostly in how fulfilling they are overall, but relatedness carries a little variance of its own. These components are dimensions of a day. The types of days come from the clustering in Section 6a.

Scores for every day

Test scores use the training weights, the training SDs, and the same rotation and flip.

component_scores <- function(block) {
  raw <- predict(pca, newdata = block)[, 1:n_keep, drop = FALSE]
  standardized <- sweep(raw, 2, pca$sdev[1:n_keep], "/")
  out <- sweep(standardized %*% rotation$rotmat, 2, flip, "*")
  colnames(out) <- comp_names
  out
}

train <- bind_cols(train, as.data.frame(component_scores(train_needs)))
test  <- bind_cols(test,  as.data.frame(component_scores(test_needs)))

round(rbind(train_mean = colMeans(train[comp_names]),
            train_sd   = sapply(train[comp_names], sd),
            test_mean  = colMeans(test[comp_names])), 2)
##            need_satisfaction need_frustration
## train_mean              0.00             0.00
## train_sd                1.00             1.00
## test_mean               0.04            -0.05
# days with no needs answers were filled with the training medians, so they
# all get the same two scores
unique(round(as.data.frame(train)[rowSums(is.na(train[needs])) > 0, comp_names], 2))
need_satisfaction need_frustration
3464 0.01 -0.27

Components, clusters, and the target (training days)

train %>%
  group_by(play_day_type) %>%
  summarise(days = n(), across(all_of(comp_names), ~ round(mean(.x), 2))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
play_day_type days need_satisfaction need_frustration
Smooth solo play day 2037 -0.13 -0.21
Connected play day 3986 0.28 -0.23
Frustrating play day 2654 -0.32 0.50 
round(cor(train[c(comp_names, "life_satisfaction")]), 2)
##                   need_satisfaction need_frustration life_satisfaction
## need_satisfaction              1.00              0.0              0.66
## need_frustration               0.00              1.0             -0.40
## life_satisfaction              0.66             -0.4              1.00

Need satisfaction is strongly related to life satisfaction on the same day. That is expected, and Section 7 discusses what it means for the model. Need frustration is related more weakly, and in the opposite direction. The play-day types line up with the components: frustrating play days are lower on need satisfaction and higher on need frustration. The two blocks describe overlapping but different parts of the day.

7. Feature Sets and Leakage

Feature sets A and B

Both sets share every predictor that is not in the needs block, including the six BANGS items:

  • Set A adds the six needs items.
  • Set B replaces the six needs items with their two component scores and adds the play-day type (the cluster) as a factor, as the handout defines set B.

The clustering block is a chosen set of predictors (the BANGS items), not the PCA block, as the handout allows. So the BANGS items stay in both sets, and the A versus B comparison asks two things. Do two scores carry what the six needs items carry? Does the play-day type add anything to the items it was built from?

shared <- c(bangs, day_preds, person_preds)
set_A  <- c(shared, needs)
set_B  <- c(shared, comp_names, "play_day_type")

c(A = length(set_A), B = length(set_B))
##  A  B 
## 32 29
setdiff(set_A, set_B)
## [1] "needs_autonomy_satisfied"     "needs_autonomy_frustrated"   
## [3] "needs_competence_satisfied"   "needs_competence_frustrated" 
## [5] "needs_relatedness_satisfied"  "needs_relatedness_frustrated"
setdiff(set_B, set_A)
## [1] "need_satisfaction" "need_frustration"  "play_day_type"
train_A <- train[c("life_satisfaction", set_A)]
train_B <- train[c("life_satisfaction", set_B)]
test_A  <- test[c("life_satisfaction", set_A)]
test_B  <- test[c("life_satisfaction", set_B)]

Data leakage we considered

  • The target in another form. Affective valence (r = 0.87 with life satisfaction) was removed.
    • The needs items are kept, as the proposal planned. They ask about the day’s experiences (doing what one values, feeling close to people), not about satisfaction with life. But they are answered in the same sitting, and need satisfaction correlates 0.66 with the target. Much of the model’s accuracy will come from them, and that accuracy describes what goes together on a day. It does not show that needs cause life satisfaction.
    • No block contains the target, so no cluster or component is built from it.
  • Lags. Every daily predictor is from the same day, so there is no lag that could reach forward into the next day.
  • Repeated measures. The split and the folds hold out whole people (Section 5).
  • Preprocessing. Imputation, dummy coding, and scaling are in recipes, re-learned inside each fold. The recoding in Section 3 learns nothing from the data.
  • Unsupervised structure. The clusters and components were fit on the training days only, and the test days were scored from that fit.
    • One smaller issue remains inside cross-validation. The cluster centroids, the component weights, and the medians that fill the blocks were learned from all training days, so in each fold the held-out days helped shape them.
    • The structure never uses the target, and six items fit on about 8,700 days barely move when a tenth of them are held out. So the effect on the cross-validated comparison should be negligible.
    • The test set is untouched by this.
  • Information from the future. The intake survey must come before the diary days it describes:
intake_time <- as.POSIXct(train$intake_date, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
gap_days    <- as.numeric(difftime(train$date, intake_time, units = "days"))
summary(gap_days)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
##   4.926  32.802  42.195  50.852  55.104 192.105     114
c(diary_days_before_intake = sum(gap_days < 0, na.rm = TRUE))
## diary_days_before_intake 
##                        0

8. Supervised Models

Recipes

# regularized regression: dummy columns and standardized predictors
recipe_linear <- function(dat) {
  recipe(life_satisfaction ~ ., data = dat) %>%
    step_impute_median(age, education) %>%
    step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) %>%
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
    step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

# trees: the same imputation, factors kept whole, no scaling
recipe_tree <- function(dat) {
  recipe(life_satisfaction ~ ., data = dat) %>%
    step_impute_median(age, education) %>%
    step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) %>%
    step_zv(all_predictors())
}

rec <- list(linear_A = recipe_linear(train_A), linear_B = recipe_linear(train_B),
            tree_A   = recipe_tree(train_A),   tree_B   = recipe_tree(train_B))

# prep once to check the recipes and count the columns each model sees
baked <- lapply(rec, function(r) bake(prep(r), new_data = NULL))
sapply(baked, function(b) c(columns = ncol(b) - 1, missing_left = sum(is.na(b))))
##              linear_A linear_B tree_A tree_B
## columns            54       52     32     29
## missing_left        0        0      0      0
  • Imputation. Age and education get the training median, because they are constant within a person. Everything else is imputed with five nearest neighbors, never using the target.
  • The ordered stressor factor becomes polynomial contrasts for the elastic net. The trees split it only between neighboring levels.
  • The trees do not need dummy columns or scaling.

Models and tuning grids

The handout requires a null model, a regularized regression with glmnet, and a tree ensemble. As in the course walkthrough, we fit the null model, the elastic net, and the random forest, on both feature sets, with the same 10 grouped folds and the same seeds. The folds are fit in parallel, so the random parts of each fit are fixed by the seeds list in trainControl() (Section 5), which is drawn from set.seed(559).

Reproducibility. We checked this by refitting. The null model, both elastic nets, both random forests, and every check in this section reproduce exactly.

Model method Tuning grid
Null (training mean) "null" none; it uses no predictors, so it is fit once
Elastic net "glmnet" alpha 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 (0 is ridge, 1 is the lasso) × 60 lambda values, log-spaced from 10^-4 × to 10 × the smallest lambda that zeroes every coefficient
Random forest "ranger" mtry 2, √p, p/3, p/2, p (rounded, p = predictor count of that set) × min.node.size 5, 20, 50, 100, 200; splitrule = "variance"; 500 trees; impurity importance; respect.unordered.factors = "order", so an unordered factor’s levels are sorted by their mean life satisfaction before each split (ranger’s default would split them in their stored order). The first run used mtry up to p/2 and min.node.size 5, 20, 50. The best values were at the top edge (node size 50 for both sets, mtry p/2 for set B), so p, 100, and 200 were added

A helper reports whether each best tuning value is inside its grid or at an edge. A best value at an edge would mean the grid should be widened.

edge_check <- function(fit) {
  sapply(names(fit$bestTune), function(v) {
    vals <- sort(unique(fit$results[[v]]))
    b    <- fit$bestTune[[v]]
    if (length(vals) == 1) "fixed"
    else if (b == min(vals)) "lowest value tried"
    else if (b == max(vals)) "highest value tried"
    else "interior"
  })
}

# fit a model, or read the saved fit. set.seed(559) stays right before each
# train() call, as in the walkthrough; the seeds in `ctrl` are what fix the
# parallel fits
fit_dir <- out_path("model_fits")
dir.create(fit_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# The recipe's column selectors keep a link to the R session they were made
# in, so a saved fit can carry a copy of every object in the session (over
# 100 MB a file). Pointing them at the global environment before saving keeps
# each file small. Nothing after the fit uses that link: the cross-validated
# results and the predictions are unchanged.
drop_session <- function(x) {
  if (rlang::is_quosure(x)) return(rlang::quo_set_env(x, globalenv()))
  if (is.list(x) && !is.data.frame(x)) {
    a <- attributes(x)
    x <- lapply(x, drop_session)
    attributes(x) <- a
  }
  x
}

fit_or_load <- function(name, expr) {
  file <- file.path(fit_dir, paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (!refit_models && file.exists(file)) return(readRDS(file))
  fit <- expr                       # evaluated here, so the fit runs only when needed
  fit$recipe$steps <- lapply(fit$recipe$steps, drop_session)
  saveRDS(fit, file)
  fit
}

# fit the folds in parallel: caret sends each fold to its own R worker. The
# seeds in `ctrl` (drawn from set.seed(559)) fix the random parts of each
# fit whatever the number of cores. Two cores
# are left free for the rest of the computer.
n_workers <- max(1, min(n_folds, parallel::detectCores() - 2))
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(n_workers)
registerDoParallel(cl)

Null model

fit_null <- fit_or_load("null", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$linear_A, data = train_A, method = "null", trControl = ctrl)
})

TrainRMSE TrainRsquared TrainMAE method

Elastic net

lambda_grid <- function(b) {
  x <- as.matrix(b[names(b) != "life_satisfaction"])
  lambda_max <- max(glmnet(x, b$life_satisfaction, alpha = 1)$lambda)
  10^seq(log10(lambda_max) - 4, log10(lambda_max) + 1, length.out = 60)
}

fit_glmnet_A <- fit_or_load("glmnet_A", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$linear_A, data = train_A, method = "glmnet", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                               lambda = lambda_grid(baked$linear_A)))
})
fit_glmnet_B <- fit_or_load("glmnet_B", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$linear_B, data = train_B, method = "glmnet", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                               lambda = lambda_grid(baked$linear_B)))
})

rbind(A = cbind(fit_glmnet_A$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_glmnet_A))),
      B = cbind(fit_glmnet_B$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_glmnet_B))))
alpha lambda alpha lambda
A 0.25 0.8518604 interior interior
B 0.75 0.3087450 interior interior

Elastic net: cross-validated RMSE across lambda, one line per alpha (feature set A).

Random forest

# widened after the first run (see the table above): p added to mtry, and
# 100 and 200 added to min.node.size
rf_grid <- function(p) {
  expand.grid(mtry = sort(unique(pmax(2, round(c(2, sqrt(p), p / 3, p / 2, p))))),
              splitrule = "variance",
              min.node.size = c(5, 20, 50, 100, 200))
}
p_A <- ncol(baked$tree_A) - 1
p_B <- ncol(baked$tree_B) - 1

fit_rf_A <- fit_or_load("rf_A", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$tree_A, data = train_A, method = "ranger", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = rf_grid(p_A), num.trees = 500, importance = "impurity",
        respect.unordered.factors = "order",
        num.threads = 1)   # one thread per fold; the folds already run in parallel
})
fit_rf_B <- fit_or_load("rf_B", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$tree_B, data = train_B, method = "ranger", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = rf_grid(p_B), num.trees = 500, importance = "impurity",
        respect.unordered.factors = "order",
        num.threads = 1)
})

rbind(A = cbind(fit_rf_A$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_rf_A))),
      B = cbind(fit_rf_B$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_rf_B))))
mtry splitrule min.node.size mtry splitrule min.node.size
A 6 variance 5 interior fixed lowest value tried
B 14 variance 50 interior fixed interior 
ggplot(fit_rf_A)

Random forest: cross-validated RMSE across mtry and minimum node size (feature set A).

Edges. The edge labels in the tables above show whether each best tuning value was inside its grid. Both elastic nets’ best alpha and lambda are inside the grid.

# set A's forest at its best mtry, across node sizes (used below)
rf_A_nodes <- filter(fit_rf_A$results, mtry == fit_rf_A$bestTune$mtry)

The random forest. Its grid was widened after the first run’s best values landed on the top edge (see the grid table).

  • Set B’s best values are inside the wider grid: mtry = 14 with node size
  • Set A’s best node size is now 5, the bottom of the grid and ranger’s default for regression (with mtry = 6).
  • At that mtry, the RMSE barely changes from node size 5 to 50 (14.839 to 14.885). Set A’s best forest is 0.21 RMSE behind the best elastic net, so smaller nodes would not change the ranking.

The cross-validated comparison

Every model used the same folds, so resamples() lines them up fold by fold.

fits <- list(null = fit_null,
             glmnet_A = fit_glmnet_A, glmnet_B = fit_glmnet_B,
             rf_A = fit_rf_A, rf_B = fit_rf_B)

model_label <- c(null = "Null", glmnet = "Elastic net", rf = "Random forest")

results_cv <- resamples(fits)
summary(results_cv)$statistics$RMSE |> round(3)

The table the report needs: one row per model and feature set, with the mean over the folds and the fold-to-fold spread (SD) of each metric.

# per-fold values of one metric, one column per model
fold_values <- function(metric) {
  v <- results_cv$values[, grep(paste0("~", metric, "$"), names(results_cv$values))]
  names(v) <- sub(paste0("~", metric), "", names(v))
  v
}

rmse_folds <- fold_values("RMSE")
r2_folds   <- fold_values("Rsquared")
mae_folds  <- fold_values("MAE")

cv_table <- data.frame(
  model       = unname(model_label[sub("_.*", "", names(rmse_folds))]),
  feature_set = ifelse(names(rmse_folds) == "null", "none", sub(".*_", "", names(rmse_folds))),
  RMSE        = colMeans(rmse_folds),
  RMSE_SD     = apply(rmse_folds, 2, sd),
  Rsquared    = colMeans(r2_folds),      # NA for the null model: its predictions do not vary
  Rsquared_SD = apply(r2_folds, 2, sd),
  MAE         = colMeans(mae_folds),
  MAE_SD      = apply(mae_folds, 2, sd),
  row.names   = NULL) %>%
  arrange(RMSE)

Did the unsupervised features help? Set A versus set B, fold by fold

The same folds scored both feature sets, so the fair comparison is within each fold. For each model, the difference is set A’s fold RMSE minus set B’s on the same fold, as in the course walkthrough:

  • A positive difference means set B did better (lower RMSE) on that fold.
  • The difference counts as larger than the fold-to-fold variability if its mean is more than two standard errors from zero. The standard error is the SD of the 10 fold differences divided by the square root of 
# each fit's fold RMSEs, in fold order
fold_rmse <- function(fit) fit$resample[order(fit$resample$Resample), "RMSE"]

# A minus B on each fold
ab <- data.frame(
  fold   = sort(fit_glmnet_A$resample$Resample),
  glmnet = fold_rmse(fit_glmnet_A) - fold_rmse(fit_glmnet_B),
  rf     = fold_rmse(fit_rf_A)     - fold_rmse(fit_rf_B))

ab %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

Fold07 -0.107 -0.145

diffs  <- ab[-1]
a_vs_b <- data.frame(
  model          = unname(model_label[names(diffs)]),
  RMSE_A         = sapply(names(diffs), function(m) mean(fold_rmse(fits[[paste0(m, "_A")]]))),
  RMSE_B         = sapply(names(diffs), function(m) mean(fold_rmse(fits[[paste0(m, "_B")]]))),
  A_minus_B      = colMeans(diffs),
  sd_diff        = apply(diffs, 2, sd),
  two_SE         = 2 * apply(diffs, 2, sd) / sqrt(nrow(diffs)),
  folds_B_better = colSums(diffs > 0),
  row.names      = NULL)
a_vs_b$beyond_noise <- abs(a_vs_b$A_minus_B) > a_vs_b$two_SE

Checking the cluster and component choices

The number of clusters and the number of components were chosen in Section 6 from the elbow, the silhouette, and the eigenvalue rules. This section checks those choices against the alternatives: K = 2 and K = 4 clusters, and one or three components. Everything here uses the training days and the same 10 folds. The test set is not touched.

Each check refits the final model type, the elastic net on set B, with one piece of set B swapped and everything else held fixed.

# set B with one piece swapped; NULL leaves that piece out
set_B_variant <- function(types = train$play_day_type,
                          needs_block = train[comp_names]) {
  d <- train[c("life_satisfaction", shared)]
  if (!is.null(needs_block)) d <- bind_cols(d, needs_block)
  if (!is.null(types)) d$play_day_type <- types
  d
}

# the same recipe, grid, folds, and seed as fit_glmnet_B
fit_glmnet_check <- function(name, d) {
  fit_or_load(name, {
    r <- recipe_linear(d)
    b <- bake(prep(r), new_data = NULL)
    set.seed(559)
    train(r, data = d, method = "glmnet", trControl = ctrl,
          tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                                 lambda = lambda_grid(b)))
  })
}

# fold-by-fold comparison with the chosen version, read like A minus B:
# chosen minus variant on each fold, so positive = the variant did better
check_table <- function(fit_list, chosen) {
  ref <- fold_rmse(fit_list[[chosen]])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fit_list), function(n) {
    r <- fold_rmse(fit_list[[n]])
    d <- ref - r
    data.frame(variant = n, RMSE = mean(r),
               Rsquared = mean(fit_list[[n]]$resample$Rsquared),
               chosen_minus_variant = mean(d),
               two_SE = 2 * sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)),
               folds_variant_better = sum(d > 0))
  })) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
}

Clusters: K = 2, 3, and 4

The K = 2 and K = 4 types are named by rules, like the K = 3 types:

  • K = 2. The cluster with higher autonomy is the good play day, and the other is the bad play day.
  • K = 4.
    • The highest relationships mean is the connected play day.
    • Of the rest, the lowest autonomy is the stalled play day.
    • Of the remaining two, the higher toxicity is the toxic social play day.
    • The last is the smooth solo play day.
name_k2 <- function(prof) {
  ifelse(prof$gaming_autonomy == max(prof$gaming_autonomy),
         "Good play day", "Bad play day")
}
name_k4 <- function(prof) {
  connected <- which.max(prof$gaming_relationships)
  rest      <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(prof)), connected)
  stalled   <- rest[which.min(prof$gaming_autonomy[rest])]
  rest      <- setdiff(rest, stalled)
  toxic     <- rest[which.max(prof$gaming_toxic[rest])]
  nm <- character(nrow(prof))
  nm[c(connected, stalled, toxic, setdiff(rest, toxic))] <-
    c("Connected play day", "Stalled play day", "Toxic social play day",
      "Smooth solo play day")
  nm
}

k_labels <- list(`2` = name_k2(cluster_profile(km_fits[[2]]$cluster)),
                 `3` = cluster_names,
                 `4` = name_k4(cluster_profile(km_fits[[4]]$cluster)))
k_type <- function(k) k_labels[[as.character(k)]][km_fits[[k]]$cluster]

Stability. A real type should come back when the data change a little. K-means is refit on 20 random samples of 80% of the training people. All training days are then assigned to the nearest centroid of that fit and compared with the full solution by the adjusted Rand index (1 = the same partition, 0 = chance agreement).

adjusted_rand <- function(a, b) {
  tab <- table(a, b)
  n   <- sum(tab)
  s   <- sum(choose(tab, 2))
  sa  <- sum(choose(rowSums(tab), 2))
  sb  <- sum(choose(colSums(tab), 2))
  expected <- sa * sb / choose(n, 2)
  (s - expected) / ((sa + sb) / 2 - expected)
}

train_people <- unique(train$id)
set.seed(559)
k_stability <- sapply(2:4, function(k) {
  replicate(20, {
    keep <- train$id %in% sample(train_people, round(0.8 * length(train_people)))
    sub_fit <- kmeans(train_bangs[keep, ], centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
    adjusted_rand(nearest_centroid(train_bangs, sub_fit$centers), km_fits[[k]]$cluster)
  })
})

What the check shows.

  • K = 2 separates good play days from bad ones. It has the highest silhouette (0.292), but it hides the difference between connected and solo play. K = 3 recovers that difference, and the two good types differ in life satisfaction.
  • K = 4 is a finer cut. It splits the frustrating play days into a toxic social type and a stalled type. These are the days with the “toxic competitive” and “low improvement” sessions the proposal expected. It also moves some connected play days into the toxic social type. The criteria do not support the extra split:
    • the silhouette is no better (0.211 against 0.218 at K = 3);
    • the solution is less stable (mean adjusted Rand 0.911 against 0.972);
    • it explains little more of life satisfaction (R² = 0.108 against 0.093).
  • K = 3 is kept. It is as stable as K = 2 (mean adjusted Rand 0.972 against 0.970), it sits at the elbow, and its types are distinct enough to name.
  • The number of clusters does not change prediction. Every version is within 0.004 RMSE of the chosen one, and the largest two-SE band is 0.021. Dropping the play-day type entirely changes nothing either. The clusters are built from the six BANGS items, and set B already contains those items. So the play-day type describes the days but gives the model nothing new.

Components: one, two, or three

# scores for m components, built the same way as the chosen two:
# standardized, varimax-rotated when m > 1, and flipped so the strongest
# loading is positive
pca_alternative <- function(m) {
  L <- pca$rotation[, 1:m, drop = FALSE] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:m], m)
  rotmat <- diag(m)
  if (m > 1) {
    v <- varimax(L)
    L <- unclass(v$loadings)
    rotmat <- v$rotmat
  }
  fl <- sign(apply(L, 2, function(l) l[which.max(abs(l))]))
  L  <- sweep(L, 2, fl, "*")
  colnames(L) <- paste0("C", 1:m)
  sc <- sweep(predict(pca, newdata = train_needs)[, 1:m, drop = FALSE],
              2, pca$sdev[1:m], "/")
  sc <- sweep(sc %*% rotmat, 2, fl, "*")
  colnames(sc) <- colnames(L)
  list(loadings = L, scores = as.data.frame(sc), communality = rowSums(L^2))
}

What the check shows.

  • One component loses information about frustration. It carries only 43% of the variance in autonomy frustration, against 71% with two.
  • Two components predict better than one. The one-component model’s RMSE is 0.243 higher, with a two-SE band of 0.13. Two components did better in 9 of the 10 folds. The gain is small, but it is consistent and larger than the fold-to-fold noise.
  • Three components and the six raw items add nothing. Both are within noise of the two components. Two scores carry what the six items carry.
  • The needs block matters. Without it, the cross-validated R² falls from 0.623 to 0.371.
  • Two components are kept. The scree plot, the eigenvalue rule at 1, and parallel analysis favor one, and the 80% rule favors three. The walkthrough’s eigenvalue cutoff, self-determination theory’s split of satisfaction from frustration, and this check all favor two.

Choosing the final model

The rule:

  1. Take the model with the lowest mean cross-validated RMSE.
  2. If a simpler model is within two standard errors of it, fold by fold, take the simpler model instead. The elastic net is simpler than the random forest, and set B (fewer columns) is simpler than set A.

The rule was set before the test set was opened.

complexity <- c(glmnet_B = 1, glmnet_A = 2, rf_B = 3, rf_A = 4)
cand <- names(complexity)

mean_rmse <- sapply(cand, function(k) mean(fold_rmse(fits[[k]])))
best <- names(which.min(mean_rmse))

# how far each model's RMSE is above the best one's, fold by fold
# (zero for the best model itself), and the 2 SE of those differences
above_best <- sapply(cand, function(k) {
  d <- fold_rmse(fits[[k]]) - fold_rmse(fits[[best]])
  c(diff = mean(d), two_SE = 2 * sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))
})
within_noise <- cand[above_best["diff", ] <= above_best["two_SE", ]]
final_key <- within_noise[which.min(complexity[within_noise])]

data.frame(model = cand, mean_RMSE = round(mean_rmse, 3),
           RMSE_above_best = round(above_best["diff", ], 3),
           two_SE = round(above_best["two_SE", ], 3),
           within_noise = cand %in% within_noise, row.names = NULL)
model mean_RMSE RMSE_above_best two_SE within_noise
glmnet_B 14.629 0.000 0.000 TRUE
glmnet_A 14.649 0.020 0.059 TRUE
rf_B 14.991 0.362 0.245 FALSE
rf_A 14.839 0.210 0.250 TRUE 
c(lowest_RMSE = best, final_model = final_key)
## lowest_RMSE final_model 
##  "glmnet_B"  "glmnet_B"
final_fit <- fits[[final_key]]

The final model is the Elastic net on feature set B.

The final model’s coefficients (training fit)

The recipe standardizes every column, including the dummy columns. So each coefficient is the change in life satisfaction (0 to 100) for one standard deviation of that column, with every other predictor held fixed. A coefficient of zero means the penalty dropped that column (its lasso part, since alpha = 0.75).

The worst-stressor columns. stress_worst is an ordered factor, so step_dummy() codes it with polynomial contrasts:

  • stress_worst_1 is a linear trend across None < Not very < Somewhat < Very;
  • stress_worst_2 is a quadratic bend;
  • stress_worst_3 is a cubic wiggle.

These three coefficients do not line up with the levels, so the table below translates them. It predicts one training day four times, changing only the worst stressor. The model is linear, so the differences are the same for any day.

final_train <- if (grepl("_A$", final_key)) train_A else train_B

# a day with no missing values, so the imputation step changes nothing
one_day <- final_train[complete.cases(final_train), ][rep(1, nlevels(train$stress_worst)), ]
one_day$stress_worst <- factor(levels(train$stress_worst),
                               levels = levels(train$stress_worst), ordered = TRUE)
level_pred <- predict(final_fit, newdata = one_day)

stress_level_effects <- train %>%
  filter(!is.na(stress_worst)) %>%
  group_by(stress_worst) %>%
  summarise(days = n(), mean_life_sat = round(mean(life_satisfaction), 1),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(raw_gap_vs_none   = round(mean_life_sat - mean_life_sat[1], 1),
         model_gap_vs_none = round(level_pred - level_pred[1], 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame()

stress_worst days mean_life_sat raw_gap_vs_none model_gap_vs_none
None 7470 68.2 0.0 0.0
Not very 131 63.8 -4.4 -0.8
Somewhat 637 55.0 -13.2 -3.4
Very 436 38.7 -29.5 -7.8
  • The raw gap is the difference in mean life satisfaction from days with no stressful event.
  • The model gap is the same difference with every other predictor held fixed.
  • The model gap is much smaller. A day with a very stressful event is 29.5 points lower on average, but only 7.8 points lower once needs, sleep, and the rest are held fixed. Stressful days also have worse needs and sleep, and those predictors take their share.
  • The decline is curved. A mild stressor barely changes the prediction, and the drop grows at “Somewhat” and “Very.”

9. The Test Set

This section runs once, after the final model was chosen above.

                        predicted = predict(final_fit, newdata = test_final))

test_perf <- postResample(test_pred$predicted, test_pred$observed)
null_test <- postResample(rep(mean(train$life_satisfaction), nrow(test_pred)),
                          test_pred$observed)

final_folds <- final_fit$resample
round(sapply(final_folds[c("RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE")], range), 3)
##        RMSE Rsquared    MAE
## [1,] 12.811    0.542  9.679
## [2,] 16.566    0.757 12.058

The test result. The final model was run once on the 3,730 test days, from people it never saw in training.

  • RMSE 14.79 on the test days, against 14.63 in cross-validation. R² 0.575 against 0.623, and MAE 11.12 against 11.12.
  • All three are inside the range of the 10 folds (RMSE 12.81 to 16.57, R² 0.542 to 0.757). The cross-validated estimate held up on new people.
  • Predicting the training mean for every test day gives an RMSE of 22.43 (the SD of life satisfaction in the test days is 22.39). The final model’s typical error is 34% smaller.
  • A typical error of about 11 points on the 0 to 100 scale is enough to flag days that are likely to be low. It is too coarse to rank two days that are close.

10. Compare and Interpret

Did the unsupervised features help? Look at the A versus B table in Section 8:

  • For every model, compare A_minus_B with two_SE (a positive A_minus_B means set B had the lower RMSE). Set B was within fold-to-fold noise of set A for every model.
  • Set B swaps six needs items for two scores and adds a three-level play-day type. Set B matches set A, so the two components carry what the six items carry, in a third of the columns.
  • The play-day type adds nothing on top of the BANGS items it was built from, because both sets keep those items. The check in Section 8 shows the elastic net does as well without it, at any K.

Do the clusters and components mean something for the research question?

  • Need satisfaction is the strongest single correlate of life satisfaction in the training days (r = 0.66).
  • Frustrating play days have the lowest mean life satisfaction.
  • The final model leans on the components. Its two largest coefficients (Section 8) are need satisfaction (13.2 points per SD) and need frustration (-7.5). The penalty set both play-day-type columns to zero. The variable importance in Section 9 shows the same ranking.

What a model of days can tell the users, and what it cannot.

  • What it can tell them. A well-being check-in could combine a few in-game questions with a short needs check. It would flag days that are likely to be low in life satisfaction for that player. A frustrating play day is one marker.
  • What it cannot tell them. About 73% of the variation in life satisfaction is between people. A model of days cannot say which players are generally less satisfied with their lives, or why. That question needs a model of people, with person-level averages and traits as the unit.
  • Same-day caveat. Because every predictor is from the same day, the model describes what goes together. It does not forecast tomorrow.

Which model to hand over, and what is lost.

  • The final model is the Elastic net on set B. It also had the lowest cross-validated RMSE, so no accuracy was given up for readability.
  • It can be shared as a list of coefficients, with the direction and size of every effect. Nothing is lost in interpretability.
  • The random forest did slightly worse (best cross-validated RMSE 14.84, against 14.63), and it would give users only importance rankings.

11. Save the Results

results <- list(
  counts = counts, solo_rule = solo_rule, split_sizes = split_sizes, icc = icc, n_folds = n_folds,
  miss_table = miss_table, intake_missing = intake_missing, var_table = var_table,
  k_choice = k_choice, k_final = k_final, cluster_names = cluster_names,
  cluster_profile = cluster_profile(km$cluster), km = km,
  n_comp_rules = n_comp_rules, n_keep = n_keep, loadings = loadings,
  rotated = rotated, comp_names = comp_names,
  k_profiles = k_profiles, k_stability_table = k_stability_table,
  check_k_table = check_k_table, type_coefs = type_coefs,
  pc_communality = pc_communality, check_pc_table = check_pc_table,
  set_A = set_A, set_B = set_B,
  cv_table = cv_table, cv_long = cv_long, ab = ab, a_vs_b = a_vs_b,
  best_tune = lapply(fits, `[[`, "bestTune"),
  edges = lapply(fits[-1], edge_check),
  final_key = final_key)

if (exists("final_coefs")) {
  results$final_coefs <- final_coefs
  results$stress_level_effects <- stress_level_effects
}

if (run_test_set) {
  results$test_perf <- test_perf
  results$null_test <- null_test
  results$test_pred <- test_pred
  results$vi_table  <- vi_table
}

saveRDS(results, out_path("final_results.rds"))

# all models are fit; shut down the parallel workers
stopCluster(cl)
registerDoSEQ()
